searches.note: Twenty three searches of a share of twenty eight, five left unspent, none of them the author's; one call on Rockford ran two searches in one batch and is counted as two. Six were restricted to a house's own domain (penfolds.com once, henschke.com.au twice, seppeltsfield.com.au three times) and are read as primary through their summaries; the rest kept the house's domain out, and where the author had leant on them Wikipedia, Langton's and J.J. Buckley, so that each second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The making and the sites went first to the house's own pages and the sheets merchants carry; the history went to the Australian Dictionary of Biography, Wikipedia and the trade with the house's domain kept out, so that each date found its second source elsewhere.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check, or in one only that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less, and the house's own claims are told as its record.

The dead are named with their dates where two sources agree (Christopher Rawson Penfold, 1811 to 1870, by the ADB and Professional Historians Australia; Max Schubert, 1915 to 1994; Cyril Henschke, 1924 to 1979; Joseph Ernst Seppelt, 1813 to 1868, by the ADB and Wikipedia; Samuel Smith, 1812 to 1889, by the ADB, Wikipedia and the state's pioneer vigneron profile); every living founder, heir and winemaker stays described.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, Liz Thach MW, Jane Anson, Campbell Mattinson, Ray Jordan, The Vintage Journal) are cited neither in the fragment nor as a second source here. The serving temperatures agree with the service reference: full reds 16 to 18 for the four dry reds, an aged tawny lightly chilled at 12 to 14.

tested: Christopher Rawson Penfold, 1811 to 1870, an English physician settled at Magill in 1844 with his wife, the stone cottage The Grange: the ADB (born 1811 to a Sussex vicar), Professional Historians Australia (died March 1870, aged 59) and the City of Burnside. Confirmed.
Mary Penfold ran the vineyards after 1870: one account among the results of the cottage search, with the house's history the author read. Confirmed; she stays described.

Max Schubert, chief winemaker from 1948, Bordeaux in 1950, the experimental 1951 from Magill and Morphett Vale: the house's story of Grange, Wikipedia, Langton's history. Confirmed; one account names the Honeypot vineyard at Magill in place of Morphett Vale. His dates, 1915 to 1994, rest on the author's two sources (Wikipedia and the house) and were not searched again here.

The 1951 was never sold: Langton's history and a vintage guide say it was never released commercially, much of it given away, and the 1952 was the first commercial release. Retold as never sold commercially.
The order to stop in 1957, the hidden 1957, 1958 and 1959 at Magill, and the board's change of mind in time for the 1960 vintage: Langton's history, the Drinks Business and Wine Spectator. Confirmed.

Grange Hermitage: Wikipedia and a merchant's directory give the name up to the 1989 vintage, and the house's note on the 1990 says from that vintage it is labelled simply Grange. Corrected from the late 1980s.
Made in every vintage since 1951: the house's note on the 1995 calls it the 45th consecutive vintage. Confirmed.

The heritage icon: the Robb Report and a merchant's note give the National Trust of South Australia's listing of 2001, its fiftieth anniversary, and the house's note on the 2004 says it is officially listed. Retold with the body and the year.

The making: the house's notes give 16 months in barrel (2004), 17 (2011), 18 (1990, 2009, 2021) and 21 (2007), all new American oak hogsheads; the finish of fermentation in barrel is in the Robb Report and Wine Spectator; the Robb Report has open concrete fermenters with wooden boards across them, a tasting note stainless steel, and no source of this check says every component. Corrected.
Bin 95, South Australia, the blend of Shiraz with a little Cabernet (94 and 6 per cent in 2021), the regions: the house's 2021 note and the library. Confirmed.
The others (Bin 389 in barrels that held Grange, St Henri in old vats, Bin 707 in new American oak) and the traps rest on the library's reviewed record. Not contradicted.

The rules: no living name (the chief winemaker of today, a critic and a writer met among the results are kept out), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: Fermented in stainless steel tanks with header boards, or in open fermenters at Magill Estate, every component of the wine finishes its fermentation in new American oak hogsheads and then matures in them for seventeen to twenty months, by vintage, before bottling.
changed.now: Fermented on its skins in tanks with header boards, wooden boards that keep the cap under the juice, the wine is racked into new American oak hogsheads to finish its fermentation and then matures in them for sixteen to twenty one months, by vintage, before bottling.
changed.why: The house's own notes run from 16 months to 21; the first vessel differs by account, and every component rested on no source.

tested: The founder, a Silesian stonemason and wheelwright, in South Australia from 1841: the house's history and a merchant's guide; Wikipedia gives a first vineyard at Keyneton about 1862, and one account dates the family's story to 1839. Kept at 1841, the house's year, with no year for the Keyneton land.
1868, the first wine: the house and the library. Confirmed.

The vineyard by the Gnadenberg church, planted about 1860 by Nicolaus Stanitzki, bought by the founder's son in 1891, who was the church's organist for many years: the house's history and vineyard page. Confirmed; the question's below the church becomes beside it.
About 400 metres, dry grown, own roots, the Grandfathers of about 1860: the house's vineyard page. Confirmed.
The soil: the house's pages give red-brown earth grading to deep silty loam, and thick red clay loams under a veneer of brown sandy to silty loam. Corrected from over.

Cyril Henschke, 1924 to 1979, fourth generation, the first Hill of Grace with the 1958, hand picked and fermented in open top fermenters: the ADB, the house's sheets carried by Winebow, a merchant's guide (his death in 1979). Confirmed.
Mount Edelstone, planted in 1912 by a descendant of George Fife Angas, came first: the library, Winebow, two writers' own sites (1952, not cited). Confirmed as first; the year stays out.

The oak: the house's sheets give more than half new in 2009, a third new in 2015 with some American, 13 per cent new in 2021 and all seasoned in 2022, about eighteen months, twenty in 2022. Corrected.
The drinking window: the house's guidance for the 2015 is thirty years and more with ideal cellaring; no source of this check gives forty to fifty. Corrected.
The rules: no living name (the fifth and sixth generations are described), no price, no score, nothing volatile. Sound.

The buildings: stone farm buildings, a cottage and outbuildings of the 1850s, in a merchant's history and the regional tourism body's listing. Corrected from a stone barn.

The equipment salvaged as other cellars modernised, bought or given: J.J. Buckley, Grape and Grain and two others; one account has the 1880s Bagshaw crusher found on the property, and one a destemmer of 1910. Kept as much of it, not most.
The basket press: about a hundred years old in one merchant's note and of the 1890s in one education site. Told as about a century old.
The oak: Langton's gives mainly seasoned French and American oak for about two years, another merchant's sheet 300 litre hogsheads with 2,500 litre vats. Corrected; the two years stay out.
The fruit: growers largely independent, dry grown, vines of 60 to 140 years by one listing. Confirmed.
Made in every vintage since 1984: no source of this check. Cut.
The rules: the founder, living, stays described; no price, no allocation (the library's note is left out), no score. Sound.

tested: Joseph Ernst Seppelt, 1813 to 1868, born at Wüstewaltersdorf in Lower Silesia, sailed from Hamburg in the Emmy on 9 September 1849 with his wife and three children, died on 29 January 1868: the ADB, whose entry spells him Ernest, and Wikipedia. Confirmed; emigrated becomes sailed.
1851: the house and the library; one Wikipedia article gives 1852 for the purchase. Kept as the house's account.

The eldest son, aged 21 when the business passed to him by one account returned with the ADB and Wikipedia, born 1845 by the ADB and 1846 by Wikipedia: early twenties stands. Suddenly and the unfinished winery are in no second source, and one house page has the Centennial Cellar begun in 1868 and finished in 1878; both go.

1878: the Centennial Cellar completed and a puncheon of the son's choosing set aside, not to be bottled for a century; released in 1978; a cask of every vintage since: the house's timeline and cellars page, Wikipedia. Confirmed; the five hundred litres is Wikipedia's alone and goes.

The grapes: the house's own pages read here name none for the Centennial wines; a retailer's listing and a magazine interview give Shiraz and Grenache. Kept, hedged as the house's account of recent releases; parcel by parcel goes.
The Para range: the house's Para Tawny page names Grand, Rare and 21 Year Old wines, blended and single vintage. Confirmed.
The glass: rancio, preserved fruit and exotic spice in the house's words on the 1926. Confirmed.
The serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, the Codex's reference for aged tawny. Confirmed; the author's report said 10 to 14 and is set right.
The rules: the son is described; a critic and a score met in the results are kept out; no price. Sound.

tested: Samuel Smith, 1812 to 1889, a brewer of Wareham in Dorset, in South Australia in 1847, a gardener for George Fife Angas at Angaston, thirty acres bought in 1849 and named Yalumba, an Aboriginal word for all the country around, planting by night: the ADB, Wikipedia and the state's pioneer vigneron profile. Confirmed.
His wife and five children: the ADB gives his wife and five children, a brochure of the house's agent four, and the pioneer vigneron profile two marriages. Corrected to his family.

The Signature: 1962 the first vintage, released in 1966, each vintage named for one person, more than 57 Signatories by the house's 2023 copy: Winebow, which carries the house's notes, and the house's own pages. Confirmed.

The make up of the 1962 (Eden Valley Shiraz, Oxford Landing Cabernet, French puncheons): in no source outside the house's back vintage page; one merchant's account has it labelled Galway Vintage Claret. Told as the house's record.
The modern wine from the Barossa in French and Hungarian oak, 18 months for the 2022: Winebow and a merchant. Confirmed.
The rules: no family member of today named, no price, no score. Sound.
